clue.text: How make his mark when Eric's nib's crossed?

definitions.note: a phrase describing the action; the answer is the verb itself

indicators.note: crossed suggests lines scored through and jumbled, so the letters of the named words get mixed up

blocks.note: the letters of the two words, apostrophes ignored

explanation.surface: A writer called Eric signs his name, his pen nib crossing the page.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a pen at work, which is exactly the sense of the answer; only 'crossed' is doing double duty as the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To engrave or write words on a surface is precisely how someone leaves a lasting written mark.

clue.text: Heady drink?

blocks.note: surface reading: a strong, intoxicating drink that goes to the head
setter's reading: a drink taken just before laying one's head on the pillow, its name also a cap worn on the head in bed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heady' normally means potent; here it points to the head going to bed, and to the headwear sharing the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A NIGHTCAP is a last alcoholic drink before sleep, and also a soft cap worn on the head in bed.

clue.text: Farewell . . . Pride, pomp, and — of glorious war!" (Othello)

definitions.text: Farewell . . . Pride, pomp, and — of glorious war!" (Othello)
definitions.note: a quotation with a gap; the answer fills the dash

blocks.note: the dash stands for the missing word in Othello's speech
the source: Othello's farewell to his military career in Act 3

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: you complete Othello's line. The phrase is also the origin of Elgar's 'Pomp and Circumstance' marches.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's speech reads 'Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war', the word meaning ceremonial formality and display.

clue.text: One point about various ladies put on pedestals

indicators.note: various suggests varied forms, so the word that follows is rearranged
about means going round, so the first pieces wrap around the rest

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, to be mixed
a compass point, east

explanation.surface: Various ladies are being placed on pedestals, admired from below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One point' splits into two separate pieces, I and E, which sit either side of the mixed word.
explanation.definitionFit: To set someone on a pedestal is the idiom for regarding them as perfect, the same as treating them as an ideal.

clue.text: There was always a short way for Scott's Colonel

blocks.note: ever means always, as in ever hopeful
taken as written
the abbreviation of road, a way cut short

explanation.surface: A colonel in a Walter Scott novel always had a shortcut to hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Markham EVERARD is the Parliamentarian hero of Scott's novel Woodstock; general knowledge is needed to confirm the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Markham Everard is the Roundhead colonel in Sir Walter Scott's novel Woodstock, set during the English Civil War.

clue.text: Figure for which an alumnus appears to yearn

blocks.note: old boy, a former pupil of a school
to long for something is to yearn for it

explanation.surface: A former student pines for some figure from the past.
explanation.walkthrough: OB, old boy, is the British term for a former pupil, especially of a public school.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle longer than it is wide is a geometrical shape, and shapes are figures in geometry.

clue.text: How to produce extremes of stupefaction

definitions.text: How to produce extremes of stupefaction

blocks.note: surface reading: seemingly the outermost letters of the long word, as if letters were to be picked

blocks.clueFragment: How to produce extremes of stupefaction
blocks.note: setter's reading: the way to cause stupefaction at its most extreme, by a knockout blow or shock

explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremes of' tempts you to take first and last letters, but they spell nothing useful; the clue simply describes causing utter daze.
explanation.definitionFit: To STUN is to knock someone senseless or astound them, the extreme degree of stupefaction.

clue.text: Cheeky boy's future form as a new arrival

blocks.note: fresh can mean impudent or forward
a boy grows into a man

explanation.surface: A cheeky boy's prospects as he joins a new school form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' looks like a school class, which fits a newcomer, but here it means the shape the boy will grow into.
explanation.definitionFit: A first-year student at a college or university is the latest arrival there.

clue.text: Railways coming in by way of Rock Hill are somewhat shaky

definitions.note: describes the thing; the answer is a noun for something that shakes

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: via means by way of
British Rail, the old national railway
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Railway lines entering via Rock Hill are a bit unstable.
explanation.walkthrough: BR, British Rail, was Britain's state railway in 1977. A tor is a rocky outcrop on a hilltop, common in Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: A vibrator is a device that oscillates rapidly, so it is a thing given to shaking.

clue.text: Soldier sent back gold to the prince

indicators.note: sent back means returned the other way, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: an American soldier
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A soldier returns gold to its royal owner.
explanation.walkthrough: IGOR is the hero of Borodin's opera Prince Igor, so 'the prince' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Igor, the medieval Russian ruler of Borodin's opera, is the best-known prince of that name.

clue.text: Not at first sight those of unusual perception?

definitions.text: Not at first sight those of unusual perception?

blocks.note: surface reading: people not noticed immediately, or not loved at first glance
setter's reading: people credited with second sight rather than first

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not at first sight' sounds like a delayed impression; it means having second sight, the supposed gift of seeing the future.
explanation.definitionFit: People claiming to see beyond normal senses, foreseeing events, are said to have second sight.

clue.text: Felt when weary travellers put a novel sort of hay in around the courtyard ?

definitions.note: a cryptic description of the feeling, not a synonym

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: Antic Hay is a novel by Aldous Huxley
taken as written, split to hold the next piece
a patio is a paved yard

explanation.surface: Tired travellers settle for a curious sort of hay in a courtyard, feeling expectant.
explanation.walkthrough: Huxley's 1923 novel Antic Hay supplies the odd sort of hay; travellers near the end of a journey feel eager expectation.
explanation.definitionFit: Weary travellers eagerly expect rest and arrival, and that looking-forward feeling is expectation.

clue.text: Mac's returned to the Philippines for sea-food

indicators.note: returned means sent back the way it came, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: the word with its apostrophe ignored
Philippine Islands, an abbreviation

explanation.surface: A Scot named Mac goes back to the Philippines in search of seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: SCAMPI are Norway lobsters, served in Britain fried in breadcrumbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are large prawns or langoustines eaten as a dish, a familiar kind of shellfish.

clue.text: What would one give for a most reliable worker?

definitions.text: What would one give for a most reliable worker?

blocks.note: surface reading: what price would you pay to hire such a worker
setter's reading: the idiom 'I'd give my ... for it', plus a trusted helper called one's right-hand man

explanation.walkthrough: Two idioms meet: 'I'd give my right arm for' something precious, and calling a trusted assistant your right arm.
explanation.definitionFit: One's right arm is both the proverbial sacrifice for something wanted badly and a figurative name for an indispensable helper.

clue.text: Term of significance in putting back the tee

indicators.note: putting back means placing the other way round, so the word is reversed
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: taken as written, to be turned round
pith is the core or significance of a matter

explanation.surface: A golfer finds meaning in putting back towards the tee.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf terms disguise the signals: 'putting' is the golf stroke on the surface but means placing here.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet is a descriptive name or phrase applied to someone, a kind of term or label.

clue.text: This floor shows a new way to lose rent

indicators.note: a new way suggests a different arrangement, so the letters that follow are reordered

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: A landlord's floor reveals a new way to forfeit the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: An ENTRESOL is a low storey between the ground and first floors, the French word for mezzanine.
explanation.definitionFit: An entresol is a mezzanine, an intermediate storey of a building, so a type of floor.

clue.text: Standard product of a threshing mill in Cheshire?

definitions.note: a place found in the county, signalled by the question mark

blocks.note: the usual run, as in run of the mill
threshing separates grain from the straw

explanation.surface: A rural question about what a threshing mill in Cheshire turns out.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheshire is a county in north-west England, and Runcorn is a town in it. 'Mill' echoes 'run of the mill', meaning standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Runcorn is an industrial town on the Mersey estuary, located within the county of Cheshire.

clue.text: Front-page attention was "bestowed" on his humble home

definitions.text: Front-page attention was "bestowed" on his humble home

blocks.note: surface reading: newspaper headlines; setter's reading: the title page of a novel
setter's reading: a cabin, the home named in the title of Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel

explanation.walkthrough: The quoted 'bestowed' hides Stowe, the author; the humble home is the cabin in her 1852 anti-slavery novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Tom is the enslaved hero whose cabin gives its name to Harriet Beecher Stowe's famous novel.

clue.text: Animal to pull up one sort of grass the wrong way

indicators.note: the wrong way means going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

blocks.note: to rein in a horse is to pull it up
a reed is a tall waterside grass

explanation.surface: An animal is made to pull up a kind of grass the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull up' looks like uprooting the grass, but it is the horse-rider's verb for stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic deer that draws Santa's sleigh is a mammal, a straightforward example of an animal.

clue.text: Horses with drinks to cool their spirits ?

blocks.note: first meaning: steeplechasers, horses that race over fences
second meaning: milder drinks taken after a shot of liquor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' looks like the horses' mettle, but it is liquor; the drinks follow it down.
explanation.definitionFit: Steeplechase horses are called by this name, and so are beers or water drunk straight after whisky.

clue.text: Nick's super score

blocks.note: surface reading: a man called Nick has achieved an excellent score
setter's reading: a nick or score is a cut mark, and the highest such cut on a tally is the best

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name but is a small cut, and 'score' means the same; the highest mark of that kind is first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means first-rate or excellent, literally the highest cut on a measuring scale.

clue.text: I almost love it up in Italy

definitions.note: a place found in the country

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the word is dropped
in a down clue up means reading from the bottom, so the whole is reversed

blocks.note: taken as written
the word without its final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone declares they nearly love a place in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: TIVOLI is a hill town near Rome, famous for its villas and gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: Tivoli is a town east of Rome known for the Villa d'Este fountains, so it lies in Italy.

clue.text: Ancient language is about the eye

blocks.note: c is circa, Latin for about
optic is an old word for the eye

explanation.surface: An old tongue that concerns the eye, perhaps hieroglyphs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' here is not a container signal but the abbreviation c, as in c 1900.
explanation.definitionFit: Coptic descends from the Egyptian of the pharaohs and survives as the liturgical tongue of the Coptic Church.

clue.text: Like the witches' brew, effects never vary

indicators.note: to vary is to change, so the letters are rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: The witches' cauldron in Macbeth keeps producing the same unchanging effects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never vary' seems to forbid change, yet 'vary' is the instruction to change the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The bubbling 'Double, double toil and trouble' cauldron in Macbeth is fizzing and frothing, which is to say bubbly.

clue.text: Trade leader

blocks.note: surface reading: a captain of industry or union boss
setter's reading: the proverb that trade follows the national banner, which therefore leads it

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'trade follows the flag' means commerce goes where a nation plants its colours, so the emblem leads trade.
explanation.definitionFit: A national ensign carried abroad by empire was proverbially followed by commerce, making it what goes ahead of trade.

clue.text: It's the same in epidemics

indicators.note: in tells you the letters sit inside the next word

blocks.note: letters two to five of the word

explanation.surface: Every epidemic follows the same pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: IDEM is Latin, used in references to mean the same author or source as before.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin pronoun idem, still used in citations, translates directly as 'the same'.

clue.text: Ambiguous like the Pythia or a copper god

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the chemical symbol for copper
a lar is a Roman household god

explanation.surface: Is something as ambiguous as the Delphic priestess, or rather a bronze idol?
explanation.walkthrough: The Pythia was the priestess of Apollo's oracle at Delphi, famous for answers that could be read two ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The Delphic priestess spoke prophecies with double meanings, so speech like hers is cryptic and prophetic.

clue.text: Near miss disconcerted the classes

indicators.note: disconcerted means thrown into confusion, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: A near miss in the playground unsettled the pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Seminars are teaching sessions for small groups of students, so they are a kind of class.
